target_customer: Mortgage lenders, title and escrow companies and notaries
problem: Mortgage closings involved paper documents and many parties. Snapdocs connects lenders, title agents and notaries in digital closing workflows.
business_model: B2B SaaS and per transaction fees

founders.name: Aaron King
founders.background_notes: YC page says his experience is in real estate, mortgage, networks and complex multiparty workflows; YC blog says the company started as a side project.

technical_complexity.rationale: Workflow software integrating lenders, title systems and notary scheduling; needed compliance with document rules.

defensibility.rationale: Two sided network of lenders and notaries plus integrations with loan systems raised switching costs.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: DocuSign invested in the Series C instead of copying; the company reached unicorn status in 2021.

market_need_then: Mortgage closings were paper heavy and multiparty; the need is inferred from later adoption, no 2014 metric found.

identity.logo: Lowercase s with an angular line suggesting two pieces snapping together
identity.visual_style: Orange as brand color for optimism and warmth
identity.voice_and_tone: Approachable and humble; tagline Make mortgage a snap

rebrands.why: Company said it had grown beyond document digitization

brand_strength.rationale: Company claims it supports 1 in 4 US mortgage transactions, but evidence of brand pull beyond B2B is limited.

outcome_analysis: Snapdocs built a two sided network of lenders and notaries, raised Series A through D, and hit a 1.5 billion dollar valuation in 2021 during the mortgage boom. Rates rose afterward, TrueUp records about 83 layoffs in November 2022, and Sacra estimates 2023 revenue fell 4 percent to about 102 million dollars. A third party secondary estimate of about 0.3 billion dollars exists but is unverified.
notes: Series A amount of 15M comes from Seedtable and StartupIntros aggregators; HousingWire confirms a Sequoia led Series A without amount. Series C total raised 103M per search summary, which exceeds recorded rounds by roughly 3M, so earlier seed rounds may be missing. Founding year 2012 or 2013 per sources. No dated competitor source near 2014 so list empty. Layoff and revenue figures come from third party estimates (TrueUp, Sacra). Audit fix: a 3M seed in March 2014 is recorded from Multiples.vc; Caplight dates it 2014-03-23 and StartupIntros lists it as 3M announced 2014-03-01. It rests on databases only (no press release found), so the amount, date and investor list are unverified; StartupIntros names individual angels (Aaron Harris, Bill Tai, Othman Laraki) instead of the funds, and no lead is disclosed. It also helps explain part of the roughly 3M gap in the totals noted above.
